tour.title: Gaya Street to the Waterfront: A Borneo Port on Foot
tour.summary: Four and a half kilometres and one steep hill through a rebuilt port town — a Chinese market street, the city's last colonial survivor, a hilltop lookout, the island ferry terminal, and a Sulu Sea market that turns into dinner after dark.
tour.overviewText:
Kota Kinabalu greets you with a wall of heat and a smell of salt and grilled fish. It is a small city on a narrow shelf of land between a hill and the South China Sea, and almost everyone here is passing through — on the way to Mount Kinabalu, to the islands, or, like you, to the rainforest and back. That transit-hub feeling is not an accident of geography. It is the whole story.

The city's old name was Jesselton, after Sir Charles Jessel, a director of the British North Borneo (Chartered) Company — a private trading firm that ruled this coast like a government, granted the land by treaties with the Sultan of Brunei in 1877 and the Sultan of Sulu in 1878. In 1899 the company moved its settlement here from nearby Gaya Island, built a deep-water jetty and a railway that hauled tobacco and rubber down from the interior, and made the place its trading capital. Jesselton shipped out rubber, rattan, honey and beeswax from one of the coast's best anchorages.

Then came the war. Japan occupied Borneo from 1942; a local uprising, the Jesselton Revolt of October 1943, was crushed and its leader executed. In 1945 Allied bombing flattened the town, leaving only a handful of buildings standing, which is why the city you walk through is almost entirely post-war. After 1946 the bankrupt company handed North Borneo to the British Crown, and the colony rebuilt Jesselton rather than Sandakan as its capital. In 1963 North Borneo joined Malaya, Sarawak and Singapore to form Malaysia; neighbouring Indonesia, under President Sukarno, opposed the new federation and fought a three-year undeclared war in Borneo, the Konfrontasi, which ended when Sukarno fell in 1966. The state took the name Sabah, and in 1967 Jesselton was renamed Kota Kinabalu — kota is Malay for city or fort, and Kinabalu comes from Aki Nabalu, "the revered place of the dead", the Dusun name of the mountain to the east.

Modern Sabah is one of the most mixed places in Malaysia: Kadazan-Dusun (the largest indigenous group), Bajau, Murut, Chinese — mostly Hakka — and Malays, plus a large population with roots across the Sulu Sea in the Philippines. It is majority Muslim but has one of Malaysia's biggest Christian communities, and its markets and its politics both run on that mixture. The economy rests on timber, palm oil and offshore oil and gas, with tourism now a mainstay — the five islands of the Tunku Abdul Rahman marine park sit just offshore.

The walk covers about four and a half kilometres, mostly flat waterfront with one steep hill — from the old Chinese trading street up to the town's hilltop lookout, then down along the water to the market, where you finish over grilled seafood at sunset.

Practicalities: this is equatorial heat, so start early and carry water; the Sunday market on Gaya Street runs from about six in the morning to one in the afternoon, and on other days the street is just shops and coffee. Carry small ringgit notes for the markets, dress modestly if you duck into a mosque, and check every price and opening time at the gate. Grab, the regional ride-hailing app, is cheap when the heat wins.

Come for the light, stay for dinner.
tour.difficulty: Easy to moderate. Almost all of it is flat, paved waterfront; the exception is the climb up Signal Hill, which is a genuine uphill walk with steps and no shade in equatorial heat. Do that part slowly, carry water, and expect to sweat.
tour.bestTimeOfDay: Start mid-morning — earlier on a Sunday, when the Gaya Street market runs from about 6am to 1pm and the street is closed to traffic. The clock tower and the hill are best in the softer light before the midday heat, and the waterfront and seafood market come alive from late afternoon into the evening. If your only free morning is not a Sunday, the walk still works; you just miss the street market.

stops.name: Gaya Street and the Sunday Market
stops.narration:
You are standing on the spine of old Jesselton. The street under your feet was laid out around 1902 as Bond Street, the commercial heart of a British trading town, and it has been a market street ever since; the line it follows began as a small railway track that brought rubber down from the interior estates to the wharf. The name Gaya comes from the Bajau word goyoh, meaning big, after the island offshore — the Bajau are the seafaring people of this coast, and you will meet their descendants later on this walk.

Look at the shophouses: two storeys, a shop below, a family above, a covered walkway for shade and rain. This is Chinatown — Sabah's Chinese community is mostly Hakka, migrants who came for trade and stayed — and the coffee shops here, the kopitiam, are the institution that runs the neighbourhood. A kopitiam is a traditional coffee shop: strong local coffee, kaya toast (coconut-and-egg jam on grilled bread), half-boiled eggs, cheap and fast. Order a kopi and sit down; the table is the best seat in the city.

If it is Sunday morning, the street is closed to traffic and the whole length becomes the Gaya Street Sunday Market, running from about six in the morning to one in the afternoon. Farmers from the interior — many of them Kadazan-Dusun, Sabah's largest indigenous group — and fishermen from the coast set up beside Chinese traders selling herbs, batik sarongs, antiques, cakes, flowers, footwear and, notoriously, pets. It has run for decades and it is the one place where the whole mixture of Sabah stands in a single queue for breakfast.

Two things to find. At number 51, the old Jesselton Post Office, now the Sabah Tourism Board — one of the very few structures left standing after Allied bombing destroyed the town in 1945. And in the pavement near the start of the street, a memorial stone laid by the last colonial governor, Ralph Hone, marking the first block of permanent shophouses built under the post-war plan to rebuild Jesselton from nothing. The city you are standing in is younger than it looks: almost all of it is 1950s and later.

Practically: the market is free to wander; carry small ringgit notes, the Malaysian currency, because nobody has change for a big bill. If today is not Sunday, the street is quieter but the shophouses, the coffee and the gate at the far end still stand. Walk slowly, look up at the shophouse balconies, and then head for the white clock tower on the hill to the south.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free public street and market. Bring small ringgit notes — vendors rarely have change for large bills.
stops.openingHours: The street is public and open at all times. The Sunday market runs roughly 06:00 to 13:00 and closes the street to traffic; on other days it is ordinary shops. Verify on the day.
stops.accessibility: Flat, paved and step-free along the street, but with kerbs and uneven patches. Market days are crowded and slow going with a wheelchair or a stroller.
stops.insiderTip: Order a kopi and kaya toast in one of the old coffee shops and watch the street from a table. Then find the memorial stone set into the pavement near the start of the street — it marks the post-war rebuild, laid by the last colonial governor.
stops.nextStopDirections: Walk south down Gaya Street to its end, then follow the road as it curves left and climbs for about three hundred and fifty metres. The white clock tower stands on the bluff ahead of you, above the shophouse roofs.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Ralff Nestor Nacor, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Atkinson Clock Tower
stops.narration:
Look up at the small white tower on the hill. This is the Atkinson Clock Tower, and it is the oldest standing structure in the city — which tells you how thoroughly the rest of the city was erased. It went up in 1905 as a memorial to Francis George Atkinson, Jesselton's first district officer, who died of malaria — "Borneo fever" — in December 1902, aged twenty-eight. His mother, Mary Edith Atkinson, gave the town a two-faced clock in his memory, and friends, together with the carpenters of visiting naval ships, raised and built the tower around it. Look at the internal carpentry if you can get close: it has the joinery of a ship's carpenter, not a builder's.

The clock itself was made by William Potts and Sons of Leeds, in England. The tower stands about fifteen metres tall, and for half a century it was far more than a memorial: it was illuminated at night and used by ships as a navigation landmark to find the harbour entrance, right up until the 1950s. Stand where you are and imagine the sea where the buildings now stand — the whole waterfront in front of you is reclaimed land, and this hill once looked straight out over the bay.

The tower is also a survivor. Japanese machine-gun fire damaged its dial and mechanism during the Second World War, and in 1945 Allied bombing destroyed almost the entire town around it; this tower and the old post office on Gaya Street were among the few things left standing. When the clock broke, it was repaired by a local firm, Yick Ming Watch Dealers, whose family has kept it running ever since, father to son. In a city rebuilt from rubble, this is the one object that has watched the whole story.

There is no ticket and no gate; the tower stands in the open and you can walk right up to it. It is a small site, a few minutes at most, on a road that climbs — this lane was once Atkinson Drive, named for the man himself. When you have had enough, turn uphill and follow the road and steps toward the viewpoint on top of the ridge. It is a real climb in this heat, but a short one.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free. It stands in the open with no ticket office and no gate.
stops.openingHours: Open access at all times. Best seen in daylight; it is a small unlit monument.
stops.accessibility: Not step-free: the tower sits on a hill with a steep approach and a few steps. The patch at the base is level once you are there.
stops.insiderTip: If the door is open, look at the internal carpentry — it has the hallmarks of a ship's carpenter — and remember the clock was made in Leeds. Then turn around and picture the sea where the reclaimed waterfront now is.
stops.nextStopDirections: From the tower, keep climbing. Follow the road and the steps up the ridge for about seven hundred metres, following the signs for the Signal Hill viewpoint. It is steep and unshaded, so take it slowly and carry water. The observation tower on top is the next stop.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: shankar s. from Dubai, united arab emirates, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Signal Hill Observation Deck
stops.narration:
You have climbed to Bukit Bendera — Flag Hill, the ridge that splits the city from the sea. It is called Signal Hill because this is where signals were raised and flags flown over the harbour below, and it explains the shape of the town: Kota Kinabalu is squeezed onto a narrow strip of flat land between this hill and the water, so when it needed more room it simply built out into the sea. Almost everything between you and the waterline is reclaimed land.

Read the view. Straight out is Gaya Island, the largest of the five islands of the Tunku Abdul Rahman marine park — a fifteen-square-kilometre lump of rainforest with coral reefs around it and a stilt village of mostly undocumented Filipino families on its far side. Beyond it the South China Sea runs to the horizon: the same water that made this bay a natural harbour and, for a century, the whole point of the settlement. To the east, on a clear morning, you can make out the blue shape of Mount Kinabalu, about fifty kilometres away and 4,095 metres high, the tallest mountain in Malaysia and the one this city is named after. In the Dusun language it is Aki Nabalu, "the revered place of the dead", the resting place of ancestors.

The geography explains the weather. Sabah calls itself Negeri di Bawah Bayu, "the land below the wind", because it sits just south of the typhoon belt that batters the Philippines and Vietnam. That luck is why this coast could be settled, farmed and shipped from at all. What it does not escape is heat and rain: equatorial, humid, with sudden afternoon downpours and spectacular evening cloud.

The viewpoint is free and open, with a small observation tower, railings and benches. Go carefully on the steps and the steep road — they are slippery after rain and there is little shade. The best light is late afternoon, when the sun drops toward the sea and the whole harbour turns gold. If you can, time your walk so you are up here for it, then head back down toward the ferry terminal on the waterfront.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free public viewpoint, open at all hours. Nothing to pay.
stops.openingHours: Open access at all times. Best in daylight; the hour before sunset is the reward. Take care on wet steps.
stops.accessibility: Not step-free: a steep road and steps all the way up, with little shade. The platform itself is level once you reach it.
stops.insiderTip: Time it for the hour before sunset, when the harbour turns gold and the islands go dark. On a clear morning you can pick out Mount Kinabalu to the east instead.
stops.nextStopDirections: There is no short way down: the observatory sits on the ridge with no direct path north, so retrace your steps down Jalan Bukit Bendera Upper and Jalan Dewan to the bottom of the hill, then turn north along Jalan Pantai and Jalan Haji Saman. It is about a kilometre and three-quarters, allow twenty-five minutes. The ferry terminal with its blue roofs and moored boats is on the waterfront ahead.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Putera Fazil, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Jesselton Point and the Waterfront
stops.narration:
This is Jesselton Point, where the city began as a port and where it still sends people to sea. The jetty takes its name from Jesselton, the town's colonial name, and the town took its name from Sir Charles Jessel, a director of the British North Borneo (Chartered) Company. That company is the strangest fact in this city's history: a private British trading firm granted the right to govern and develop this whole coast by treaties with the Sultan of Brunei in 1877 and the Sultan of Sulu in 1878, which then ran it — taxes, police, railways — as a business for sixty years. In 1899 it moved its settlement here from Gaya Island, built this harbour and a railway up into the interior, and made Jesselton the trading capital of North Borneo. Rubber, rattan, honey, beeswax and tobacco all left through this waterfront.

Today the jetty is the departure point for the Tunku Abdul Rahman marine park — five islands: Gaya, Sapi, Manukan, Mamutik and Sulug, gazetted as a park in 1974 and named after Tunku Abdul Rahman, Malaysia's first prime minister. Two-thirds of the park is sea: coral reef, white sand, snorkelling. Boats leave roughly hourly from about eight in the morning, the last returns are around four in the afternoon, and you must book your return time when you buy your ticket. Expect a small terminal fee, a return boat fare in the region of thirty-five ringgit and a park admission fee on top for non-Malaysians — but prices move, so verify every figure at the counter before you pay, and carry cash.

The larger point is on the water itself. The Sulu Sea and the South China Sea were one connected trading world long before there was a border between Malaysia and the Philippines; families, languages and boats crossed it freely, and they still do. That is why the market a few hundred metres along this waterfront is full of Sulu Sea faces, and why the Philippines has never entirely dropped its old claim to Sabah, inherited from the Sultanate of Sulu. Nobody here is a stranger to the sea.

From the terminal, walk south along the waterfront. The promenade is flat, shaded in places and lined with cafes, and the walk to the market takes fifteen to twenty minutes.
stops.entranceFeeTry: Free to visit; island trips from about RM35
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free to walk the terminal and waterfront. Island trips cost separately — a terminal fee of a few ringgit, a return boat fare of about RM35 and a park admission fee for non-Malaysians. Prices move; verify at the counter and carry cash.
stops.openingHours: The ferry terminal operates daily, roughly 08:00 to 17:00, with the last island returns around 16:00. The waterfront itself is open at all hours. Verify boat times at the counter on the day.
stops.accessibility: Level paved waterfront and terminal concourse. Boarding the boats involves steps and a moving deck; staff assist.
stops.insiderTip: Buy your return ticket with a fixed time slot when you arrive, and keep the paper — the boats are scheduled, and an after-hours pickup is expensive. The islands are quietest on weekdays.
stops.nextStopDirections: Turn south and walk along the waterfront promenade for fifteen to twenty minutes, past the cafes and the central fish market, until the craft stalls begin. The Filipino Market, also called the Handicraft Market, is the next stop.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: CEphoto, Uwe Aranas, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Filipino Market (Handicraft Market)
stops.narration:
You have reached the market everyone calls the Filipino Market, though its other name is the Handicraft Market — Pasar Kraftangan in Malay. Both names are true. It is where you buy souvenirs, and it is where many of the sellers are Filipino: Bajau, Sama and Tausug families whose roots are in the Sulu Archipelago across the sea to the north-east, part of the same Sama-Bajau world that has fished and traded these waters for centuries.

Understand who the Bajau are, because they matter here. They are a seafaring people, historically boat-dwelling, spread across the southern Philippines, Sabah and eastern Indonesia; the boat-dwelling among them call themselves Bajau Laut, the sea Bajau. They were the sailors and fishermen of the Sulu Sultanate, and today they are one of Sabah's largest ethnic groups — and also among its poorest, with many families living without documents or secure land. The market is their shopfront: a way to make a living from the sea and from the visitors the sea brings. Buy something, bargain politely, and treat the people behind the stalls as traders doing business, not as an attraction.

By day the stalls are heaped with what the region makes: South Sea pearls, batik sarongs, wood carvings, rattan baskets, T-shirts, shell craft and trinkets. Bargaining is normal and expected — start low, smile, and be ready to walk away. Prices are in ringgit, cash only, and small notes are best.

Then the light goes, and the same stretch of waterfront turns into the seafood night market. Iced trays come out: whole fish, prawns, squid, crab and shellfish, laid in rows. You choose what you want, agree the price — it is usually quoted per kilogram, so confirm the weight and the total before anything is cooked — and then it is grilled over charcoal with sambal, the chilli paste that is the backbone of Malaysian cooking, and served at plastic tables a few metres from the water. It is loud, smoky and cheap by any Western standard, and one of the best meals in Borneo. If you are unsure what is fresh, look at what the local families are buying.

The market is a piece of an older map. The Sulu Sea was a single trading region long before the colonial border was drawn across it, and this waterfront is where that history still turns up for dinner.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free to walk the market. Crafts are priced per stall and negotiable; seafood is usually sold by weight. Confirm the total before anything is cooked, and carry small notes.
stops.openingHours: Craft stalls roughly 09:00 to 18:00 daily. The seafood night market sets up from late afternoon until around 22:00 or 23:00. Hours shift with the season — verify at the stalls.
stops.accessibility: Level but crowded and uneven underfoot, with narrow aisles between stalls. Manageable, but not step-free in the busiest aisles.
stops.insiderTip: For seafood, agree the price per kilo and the total before it is cooked, and eat where the local families are eating. For crafts, bargain politely and open at about half the asking price.
stops.nextStopDirections: Walk the last few hundred metres south-west along the water, past the seafood grills, to the open stretch of promenade facing Gaya Island. That is the finish of the walk.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Bahnfrend, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Kota Kinabalu Waterfront
stops.narration:
This is the end of the walk: the reclaimed waterfront, the last of the light on the South China Sea, and dinner within arm's reach. Sit down, order the fish you chose a hundred metres back, and watch the sun drop behind Gaya Island. Kota Kinabalu does not have many grand buildings, but it has one of the great cheap sunsets of Southeast Asia, and this is the place to take it in.

Look back at what you have covered. You began on a Chinese trading street that was once a rubber railway, walked up past the town's one surviving colonial landmark, climbed the hill that explains why the city is shaped like this, crossed the waterfront where the British North Borneo Company shipped out the wealth of the interior, and finished in a market built by seafaring families from across the Sulu Sea. That is the whole city in four and a half kilometres: a port that was flattened in 1945, rebuilt as the capital of a new state in 1963, and now living on timber, palm oil, oil and gas, and the travellers who come for its islands and its rainforest.

Two things are worth a separate trip while you are here. First, the Kota Kinabalu City Mosque, out at Likas Bay — the "floating mosque", built between 1989 and 2000 on a man-made lagoon so that it appears to sit on the water, with a blue and gold dome modelled on the Prophet's Mosque in Medina and room for twelve thousand worshippers. It is a short Grab ride north of here; non-Muslims are welcome outside prayer times if you dress modestly, covering arms and legs, and the best photographs are at sunset. Second, Mount Kinabalu itself, the mountain that gave the city its name — about ninety kilometres east by road and a serious two-day climb that must be booked well in advance.

A few closing notes. The city centre is small and safe to walk by day; after dark, use Grab, the regional ride-hailing app, which is cheap and reliable. Carry small ringgit notes. And if your stay happens to include a Sunday morning, come back to Gaya Street before one o'clock — the market you walked through at the start is the best single hour this city offers.

Eat well. You have earned it.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free promenade. Seafood grills, cafes and the floating mosque trip cost separately.
stops.openingHours: Open access at all times. Liveliest from late afternoon until late evening, when the grills are lit.
stops.accessibility: Flat, wide, paved promenade — the most accessible stop on the walk. Benches and railings along the water.
stops.insiderTip: Stay past sunset: the grills stay lit, the heat finally breaks, and the lights of Gaya Island come on across the water. Then take a Grab home.
stops.nextStopDirections: End of the walk. Stay for dinner at the grills, then take a Grab back to your hotel — the centre is small and fares are low. If you have a Sunday morning left, return to Gaya Street before one o'clock; and for one more sight, the floating City Mosque at Likas Bay is a short ride north, best at sunset.
